xray.text:
**Personal Statement**

I am an assistant professor of public health at Concordia University. My research focuses on food environments and diabetes prevention in West African immigrant communities in Montreal. We partnered with community kitchens and our findings were shared widely with stakeholders. My work has been published in a high-impact journal (IF 14.2) and my h-index is 11.

**Research Contributions**

1. Food environment audit
I led the design of a two-year food-environment audit across 12 corner stores in Saint-Michel, working with three community organizations over seven years of prior relationship-building. A community advisory board was established and a screening protocol was developed. As of May 2024 the audit dataset was the only one of its kind in Quebec. The main paper has been cited 41 times and appeared in The Lancet Regional Health – Americas.

2. Diabetes prevention pilot
We developed a culturally adapted diabetes prevention program with two community kitchens. Our program could reduce screening gaps and we hope to expand it to other neighbourhoods. Sixty participants were recruited and retention was good.

I have supervised several students. In the future we hope to continue this work.

contributions.title: Corner-store food environments made visible in Saint-Michel
contributions.stakes: Diabetes risk in West African immigrant neighbourhoods is shaped by what corner stores stock, but as of May 2024 no Quebec dataset described those food environments at store level — services were planned on census proxies.
contributions.roleLine: I led the audit design and analysis; community partners led store relationships and data collection.
contributions.activities: I led the design of a two-year food-environment audit across 12 corner stores in Saint-Michel, co-developed with three community organizations after seven years of relationship-building. I trained six community data collectors and led the analysis; partners set the audit calendar and owned store consent.
contributions.outputs: A store-level food-environment dataset (community-held), a bilingual audit toolkit, the main audit paper, and a plain-language neighbourhood report distributed through partner networks.
contributions.outcomes: The regional public-health directorate added corner-store measures to its 2025 neighbourhood profiles, and two partner organizations now run the audit annually without me. The main paper has been cited 41 times in 20 months.
contributions.impact: If store-level auditing spreads to other boroughs — two have asked — food-environment data could shift diabetes prevention planning from census proxies to street-level evidence across Montreal.
contributions.translational: A Saint-Michel store owner reorganized shelf placement after seeing the audit report; the advisory board now cites it in every partner meeting.

evidence.text: Audit paper, The Lancet Regional Health – Americas (2024); cited 41 times in 20 months
Corner-store measures adopted in the DRSP 2025 neighbourhood profiles (public document)
Community-held audit dataset, annual collection cycles run by two partner organizations

contributions.title: A diabetes-prevention program that cooks where people already cook
contributions.stakes: Standard diabetes-prevention curricula assume kitchens, foods, and schedules that don't match West African immigrant households, so uptake in the communities at highest risk stays low.
contributions.roleLine: I co-led the adaptation with two community kitchens; the recipes and delivery model are theirs, the evaluation design is mine.
contributions.activities: I co-designed a culturally adapted prevention program with two community kitchens, led the evaluation design, and ran the 60-participant pilot with 82% retention at six months. Community cooks led session delivery; I led the measurement and analysis.
contributions.outputs: The adapted 12-week curriculum (community-owned), a facilitator training guide, the pilot evaluation paper (under review), and a costed scale-up brief for the regional directorate.
contributions.outcomes: Both kitchens have kept the program running past the pilot without project funding, and one has trained a second cohort of facilitators.
contributions.impact: If the pilot results hold, kitchen-based delivery could become a recognized prevention pathway for communities the clinic-based model misses — the scale-up brief is in front of the directorate now.
contributions.translational: A participant told the advisory board the program was the first time a health service had cooked her food, not lectured her about it.

evidence.text: Pilot evaluation manuscript (under review, 2026); 60 participants, 82% six-month retention
Scale-up brief submitted to the regional public-health directorate (2026)

contributions.title: Community data governance for small health datasets

mentees.why: First trainee from the partner community to join the lab; now sits on the other side of the data.
Recruited through a community kitchen, not a course.

seed.mentorPhilosophy: Every trainee presents to the community advisory board before they present at any conference — the partners hear it first, and the trainees learn who the work answers to.
seed.mentorEDI: I recruit through partner organizations as well as course lists; of seven trainees so far, five are from the communities the research serves and four are first-generation university students.

ps.field: food environments and diabetes prevention in West African immigrant communities
ps.challenge: Diabetes prevention keeps failing the communities at highest risk because the evidence describes neighbourhoods from the outside — census proxies instead of the stores, kitchens, and budgets people actually navigate.
ps.streams: Two strands: making food environments visible at street level, and adapting prevention to where people already cook. The thread is that the communities hold the data and the delivery.
ps.pivot: I came to research from a community-kitchen volunteer shift during my MPH — watching a nutrition workshop empty out taught me more than the coursework did.
ps.standing: Early signals: a Lancet Regional Health paper cited 41 times, adoption of our audit measures by the regional directorate, and a CIHR Catalyst grant (2025).
ps.programFit: The Project Grant rewards sustained community partnership and measurable prevention outcomes — both are the core of this program, and the pilot gives it the preliminary data the competition expects.
ps.horizon: Scaling the kitchen-based model across four boroughs with the directorate, with community organizations as co-applicants, not sites.

seed.consultQuestions: Is contribution 1 strong enough to lead with, or does the pilot (contribution 2) read as more fundable? And is my standing paragraph too thin for a Project Grant panel?

contributions.title: BanglaBench — the first community-validated open benchmark for Bengali NLP
contributions.stakes: Most NLP advances ride on English; as of May 2024, no open benchmark covered Bengali dialect variation, so 230 million speakers were evaluated — when at all — on translated English tasks.
contributions.roleLine: I designed the benchmark and the community-validation methodology; the dialect coverage is the translators' as much as mine.
contributions.activities: I led the design and release of BanglaBench-1.0, the first comprehensive open benchmark for Bengali natural language understanding. I personally designed the task taxonomy, recruited and trained 12 community translators across two major dialects, and authored the validation framework. Lead author on the EMNLP 2024 paper.
contributions.outputs: BanglaBench-1.0 (open source, MIT licence) with two dialect tracks and five evaluation task families, the EMNLP 2024 paper, a community-translator recruitment guide, and a dialect-coverage validation toolkit.
contributions.outcomes: BanglaBench is used by 31 research groups across five countries, including two Bangladeshi government labs, and is the named evaluation standard in a Government of Bangladesh-funded ML hub at the University of Dhaka. Cited in 18 peer-reviewed papers since late 2024.
contributions.impact: If BanglaBench becomes the de facto Bengali evaluation standard — negotiation with the open-ML community is active — it could shift low-resource NLP from English-centric leaderboards toward community-validated, language-specific evaluation.

evidence.text: EMNLP 2024 paper; outstanding-paper honourable mention; cited in 18 peer-reviewed papers
Named evaluation standard, Government of Bangladesh ML hub, University of Dhaka (2025)
BanglaBench-1.0 in use by 31 research groups across five countries

contributions.title: TamilEval — morphology-aware evaluation for one of the world's 20 biggest languages
contributions.stakes: Tamil's rich morphology breaks evaluation schemes designed for English, so open Tamil models were being scored on tasks that ignored the very structures they fail on.
contributions.roleLine: We built TamilEval across two institutions; I supervise the morphology track and hold responsibility for its evaluation design.
contributions.activities: I co-designed TamilEval-0.5 with a five-person team across Concordia and IIIT-Madras, led the morphology-aware evaluation track, and supervised one master's student through the annotation pipeline. Second author on the ACL 2025 Findings paper; primary owner of the morphology track.
contributions.outputs: TamilEval-0.5 (Apache 2.0), the ACL 2025 Findings paper, and a Tamil morphology evaluation toolkit for open-model developers.
contributions.outcomes: Adopted by three Indian research groups and by the Tamil Virtual Academy for evaluating their open-source Tamil LLM; two community annotation contributions arrived unprompted in the first six months.
contributions.impact: If TamilEval reaches v1.0 with full morphology coverage, it could become the standard open evaluation for Tamil — currently underserved relative to its 80 million speakers.

evidence.text: ACL 2025 Findings paper, selected for the Resource Track
Adopted by the Tamil Virtual Academy for their open-source Tamil LLM evaluation

contributions.title: Privacy-preserving NLP co-designed with diasporic communities (pilot)
contributions.stakes: Diasporic South Asian communities in Montréal generate text their languages' NLP tools can't serve — and the cloud tools that could serve them raise privacy costs those communities have named explicitly.
contributions.roleLine: I brought the NLP; the community partners brought the questions, the recruitment, and the instrument design.
contributions.activities: I co-designed a six-month pilot with three diasporic community organisations on what privacy-preserving on-device NLP could offer them, led the consultation workshops and the synthesis, and built the prototype. Community partners led recruitment and instrument design; one partner co-authored the methodology.
contributions.outputs: A white paper, a community-validated needs assessment, and an open-source prototype demonstrating on-device Bengali summarisation.
contributions.outcomes: One organisation has piloted the prototype with its volunteer translation team and contributed feedback toward v2; three partners are co-signing a SSHRC partnership letter of intent.
contributions.impact: This could become a working model for community-owned NLP development in diasporic contexts — a gap both the NLP and community-research literatures name but neither fills. Early-stage, and I say so.

evidence.text: White paper downloaded 230+ times in three months; two partners requested phase 2 in writing
On-device Bengali summarisation prototype (open source), piloted by one partner's translation team

mentees.why: 2024 NSERC USRA on a project we co-designed; first-generation university student.
Won a Concordia undergraduate research prize for the BanglaBench dialect work.

seed.mentorPhilosophy: Structure first, autonomy second: explicit milestone scaffolding for a new RA's first 6 weeks, then progressive handover of ownership — weekly 30-minute one-on-ones throughout, code through mandatory pair review.
seed.mentorEDI: I recruit through WiCS and the CS undergraduate society and require no prior research experience — only coursework and curiosity. Two of my four current RAs are first-generation university students.

ps.field: natural language processing for low-resource South Asian languages
ps.challenge: NLP's accuracy gap follows the training-data map: 1.7 billion South Asian language speakers face worse systems every year the field scales on data their languages don't have — and closing the gap needs evaluation standards built with the language communities, not just more scraped text.
ps.streams: Benchmarks built with communities (BanglaBench, TamilEval), and community-owned applications of them (the on-device pilot). One thread: who sets the evaluation standard controls whose language counts.
ps.pivot: I came to NLP through community translation work in my family's Bengali church-basement school; the benchmarks are that experience, formalised.
ps.standing: Two first-of-their-kind open benchmarks in active use by 30+ groups internationally, an EMNLP outstanding-paper honourable mention, and adoption by a national ML hub — two years post-PhD.
ps.programFit: The Discovery Launch Supplement exists to convert a postdoc trajectory into an independent program: the benchmarks are the track record, the community-owned NLP program is the launch.
ps.horizon: An independent Concordia program in privacy-preserving, community-co-designed NLP for diasporic South Asian communities, in partnership with the Centre for Engineering in Society.

seed.consultQuestions: Should contribution 3 (the pilot) lead, since it's where the independent program comes from — or is it too early-stage to lead an NSERC document? And does my impact framing for BanglaBench overclaim?

contributions.title: A food-security protocol the City of Montréal now builds on
contributions.stakes: Urban Indigenous food insecurity was invisible in municipal planning because no data existed that communities themselves owned and governed.
contributions.roleLine: I co-designed the protocol and led the methodology; the communities own the data and the decisions.
contributions.activities: I co-designed a longitudinal food-security protocol with three urban Indigenous organisations in Tiohtià:ke/Montréal under their OCAP data-sovereignty frameworks. I led the methodology development and analysis training across 7 years; my team led instrument adaptation; community partners led recruitment and interpretation.
contributions.outputs: A bilingual community-validated survey instrument, a 7-year community-owned longitudinal dataset with federated access, three community-authored reports, and five co-authored peer-reviewed papers.
contributions.outcomes: The protocol was adopted by the City of Montréal's 2024 Urban Indigenous Housing Strategy. Two of three partner organisations run their own annual collection cycles independent of the academic team, and the federated-access agreement is a referenced model in two other Canadian cities.
contributions.impact: Hypothesised: with the four-city SSHRC partnership now in progress, the protocol could become a national reference for community-owned urban Indigenous health data — a structural shift in who holds the evidence.

evidence.text: Cited as methodological anchor, City of Montréal Urban Indigenous Housing Strategy 2024 (public document)
Three follow-on partnership grants (SSHRC, CIHR, CFREF) totalling $4.7M built on this protocol
2023 CIHR Knowledge Translation Award

contributions.title: Eleven years of housing-precarity evidence with the Native Friendship Centre
contributions.stakes: Chronic-disease trajectories among precariously housed urban Indigenous adults were undocumented in Québec — policy ran on point-in-time counts that missed the trajectory entirely.
contributions.roleLine: I designed and led the cohort; the Centre co-governs it and its consent design is now the study's most-cited feature.
contributions.activities: I designed and led an 11-year longitudinal cohort study of housing precarity and health among urban Indigenous adults, in partnership with the Native Friendship Centre of Montréal. I personally led the recruitment protocol, the data-governance design, and the senior-author role on every major output.
contributions.outputs: Two peer-reviewed papers on chronic-disease trajectories (one in The Lancet Regional Health – Americas), an open-access policy brief, and a community-facing summary distributed through three Indigenous community centres.
contributions.outcomes: The cohort data informed Santé Québec's 2022 update to municipal Indigenous health-services planning, and three Indigenous health units in Québec have adopted the cohort-recruitment protocol.
contributions.impact: Hypothesised: the consent and data-governance design could become the default reference for urban Indigenous cohort research in Canada — closing a methodological gap this literature has named for two decades.

evidence.text: Lancet Regional Health – Americas paper cited 87 times in 24 months
Santé Québec 2022 planning update, documented in the public report

contributions.title: OCAP methodology for urban, multi-community research
contributions.stakes: OCAP principles were developed for single-community settings; urban multi-community research had no formalized application of them.
contributions.roleLine: I am the primary author of the urban OCAP methodology; community advisors govern its every revision.
contributions.activities: Our partners hold the data and our role is to serve their governance. I led a 4-year methodological project on applying OCAP in urban, multi-community contexts, with community-partner advisory throughout.
contributions.outputs: A methodological paper (Journal of Indigenous Wellbeing 2021), a peer-reviewed methods reader, and a community-protocol toolkit shared with two Indigenous Health Authority offices.
contributions.outcomes: The toolkit is a First Nations Information Governance Centre recommended supplement to OCAP training; two Tier 1 Indigenous research chairs cite it in their grant infrastructures.

evidence.text: Adopted by FNIGC as recommended OCAP training supplement (2023); cited in 41 peer-reviewed papers

contributions.title: The Chair as training infrastructure — Community Health Equity
contributions.stakes: Community-based health research fails when the people trained to do it all come from, and return to, the academy.
contributions.roleLine: I designed and lead the Chair's research and training program.
contributions.activities: Since 2018 I have led the Concordia Research Chair in Community Health Equity (Tier 1). I personally designed the Chair's research program, supervised 14 PhD students and 5 postdocs through it, and led the design of its annual community-knowledge-translation events.
contributions.outputs: Seven years of annual public symposia, three community-policy briefs, and an open-access training program in community-based research with 220+ trainees.
contributions.outcomes: Chair-trained alumni hold positions at Statistics Canada's Indigenous health unit, two Indigenous-led research organisations, McGill's Indigenous health research program, and three Québec universities. Three Chair-trained PhDs now hold Canada Research Chairs.
contributions.impact: Hypothesised: the training infrastructure is the most durable contribution — researchers I trained now set priorities for Canadian Indigenous health research, and that capacity effect compounds over decades.

evidence.text: Chair externally reviewed 2023 with strong outcomes; three alumni hold Canada Research Chairs
Training program cited as a model in two CIHR institutional reviews

contributions.title: Anti-colonial methods, from the margins to the adjudication guides
contributions.stakes: What counts as rigorous community-based health research was defined without the communities in it.
contributions.roleLine: I chaired the panels and co-authored the guidance that moved anti-colonial review criteria into national adjudication.
contributions.activities: Across my career I have been a methodological developer, senior reviewer, and chair of national review panels for anti-colonial approaches to community-based health research, including co-authoring the CIHR-commissioned guidance document (2022).
contributions.outputs: Two handbook chapters, a keynote series, and the CIHR-commissioned guidance on anti-colonial research methods.
contributions.outcomes: The guidance is referenced in Tri-Council Policy Statement consultation processes, and two national review panels I chaired have integrated anti-colonial criteria into their adjudication guides.

evidence.text: CIHR guidance document downloaded 5,400+ times; 2023 CIHR Knowledge Translation Award

seed.mentorPhilosophy: Supervision is a long-term relationship, not a transaction: once you have been my student you remain part of the lab community as long as you wish, and I expect to learn from you as your research matures past mine.
seed.mentorEDI: Of 14 PhDs completed, 5 are Indigenous, 7 racialised, 11 first-generation graduate students — recruited deliberately through community-partner networks as much as academic channels, with mandatory community-partner relationship-building from year one.
seed.mentorCrossStage: Five postdocs mentored as independent collaborators (all five now in tenure-track or research-policy positions), plus junior faculty across three Québec universities through the Chair's network.

ps.field: structural determinants of health in urban Indigenous communities
ps.challenge: Urban Indigenous health inequities are driven by structural determinants — housing, food sovereignty, the racial geographies of cities — and the policy response lags because the evidence has been held in pieces, by the wrong hands.
ps.streams: Community-owned data infrastructure; housing-precarity cohorts; anti-colonial methods. One thread: the communities own the evidence about their own health.
ps.pivot: Twenty-two years ago a community partner asked me who would own the data. The honest answer changed my methods, and then my field.
ps.standing: CRC Tier 1 since 2018; $4.7M in follow-on partnership funding; 14 PhDs and 5 postdocs trained, three now holding CRCs; 2023 CIHR Knowledge Translation Award.
ps.programFit: The Project Grant rewards sustained partnership and demonstrable uptake; this program has both, plus the training infrastructure that makes the results durable.
ps.horizon: A national community-owned data infrastructure for urban Indigenous health, under development with five sister sites and FNIGC, meeting OCAP standards while connecting to municipal and federal policy systems.
